parts.problem_md:
The times, in days, spent cocooned by 15 Monarch butterflies and 25 Common Blue butterflies were recorded. The table shows the means and the standard deviations of the times.

| **Species** | **Number of butterflies** | **Mean** | **Standard deviation** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch | 15 |   | 1.51 |
| Common Blue | 25 | 13.4 | 1.24 |

Given that the mean time for all 40 butterflies is 11.93 days, find the mean time for the Monarch butterflies and complete the table.
parts.solution_md:
Find the total time for all 40 butterflies

$40 \times 11 . 93 = 477 . 2$

**[B1]**

Subtract the Common Blue total, then divide by the 15 Monarch butterflies

$\text{Monarch total} = 477 . 2 - 25 \times 13 . 4 = 477 . 2 - 335 = 142 . 2$

$\text{Monarch mean} = \frac{142.2}{15}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **Monarch mean = 9.48 days**

**[A1]**

| **Species** | **Number of butterflies** | **Mean** | **Standard deviation** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch | 15 | **Final answer:** **9.48** | 1.51 |
| Common Blue | 25 | 13.4 | 1.24 |

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Total for all 40 butterflies of 477.2. Accept unevaluated.
> 
> **M1**: The Common Blue total (335) subtracted from the overall total and divided by 15.
> 
> **A1**: Monarch mean of 9.48.

parts.problem_md: Find the standard deviation of the times spent cocooned by all 40 butterflies.
parts.solution_md:
For each species (M for Monarch, C for Common Blue), rearrange the variance formula `\text{Variance} = \dfrac{\sum x^{2}}{n} - \left(\bar{x}\right)^{2}` to find `\sum x^{2} = n\left(\text{Variance} + \left(\bar{x}\right)^{2}\right)`

`\sum x_{M}^{2} = 15\left(1.51^{2} + 9.48^{2}\right) = 1382.2575`

**[B1]**

`\sum x_{C}^{2} = 25\left(1.24^{2} + 13.4^{2}\right) = 4527.44`

**[B1]**

Add them and use the variance formula for all 40 butterflies, whose mean is 11.93

$\text{Variance} = \frac{1382.2575+4527.44}{40} - 11 . 93^{2}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 147 . 742 \dots - 142 . 3249 = 5 . 4175 \dots$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{5.4175\dots} = 2 . 3275 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation = 2.33 days (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $\sum x^{2}$ for the Monarch butterflies of 1382.2575, or answers which round to 1380. Follow through from their mean in part (a).
> 
> **B1**: $\sum x^{2}$ for the Common Blue butterflies of 4527.44, or answers which round to 4530.
> 
> **M1**: The combined $\sum x^{2}$ divided by 40, minus 11.93 squared.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 2.33.

parts.problem_md:
Botanists are testing a new fertiliser. They grow one group of geraniums without the fertiliser (the control group) and another group with it (the experimental group), keeping all other growing conditions the same.

The heights, $h$ cm, of the 40 plants in the control group 15 weeks after planting are summarised in the table below.

| **Height (*****h***** cm)** | *h* < 10 | *h* < 15 | *h* < 20 | *h* < 25 | *h* < 30 | *h* < 35 | *h* < 40 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cumulative frequency** | 2 | 7 | 12 | 19 | 34 | 39 | 40 |

For the heights of the control group,

(i) write down the modal class,

(ii) find the class that contains the median,

(iii) find the smallest and largest possible values of the interquartile range.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

Subtract consecutive cumulative frequencies to find the frequency of each class

*Frequencies: 2, 5, 5, 7, 15, 5, 1*

The highest frequency, 15, is in the class from 25 cm to 30 cm

**Final answer:** **25 ≤ h < 30**

**[B1]**

(ii)

There are 40 plants, so the median lies between the 20th and 21st heights. 19 plants are under 25 cm and 34 are under 30 cm

**Final answer:** **25 ≤ h < 30**

**[B1]**

(iii)

The lower quartile is about the 10th height and the upper quartile about the 30th height

*Lower quartile: 7 plants are under 15 cm and 12 under 20 cm, so 15 ≤ LQ ≤ 20*

*Upper quartile: 19 plants are under 25 cm and 34 under 30 cm, so 25 ≤ UQ ≤ 30*

**[B1]**

The IQR is smallest when the upper quartile is as low as possible and the lower quartile as high as possible

$25 - 20$

**Final answer:** **Smallest possible IQR = 5 cm**

**[B1]**

The IQR is largest when the upper quartile is as high as possible and the lower quartile as low as possible

$30 - 15$

**Final answer:** **Largest possible IQR = 15 cm**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Modal class 25 ≤ h < 30. Accept "25 to 30".
> 
> **B1**: Median class 25 ≤ h < 30.
> 
> **B1**: Lower quartile located in the class 15 to 20 and upper quartile in the class 25 to 30.
> 
> **B1**: Smallest possible IQR of 5.
> 
> **B1**: Largest possible IQR of 15.

parts.problem_md:
For the experimental group, the lower quartile, median and upper quartile of the heights are 23.4 cm, 27.1 cm and 28.5 cm respectively. The shortest plant is 15.2 cm and the tallest is 33.5 cm.

Compare the heights of the plants in the two groups.
parts.solution_md:
Compare the averages: the experimental median of 27.1 cm lies in the control group's median class

**Final answer:** **On average, the plants in the two groups grew to similar heights**

**[B1]**

Compare the spread: the experimental range is 18.3 cm, but the control range is more than 25 cm, since one plant is under 10 cm and one is at least 35 cm

**Final answer:** **The heights of the plants given fertiliser are less spread out (more consistent) than those in the control group**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A comparison of the averages in context, for example that the average heights are similar because the experimental median lies in the control median class. A statement that the fertilised plants are taller on average is accepted if it is supported by a reason.
> 
> **B1**: A comparison of the spread in context, for example that the fertilised plants' heights are more consistent, supported by the range or the interquartile range.
> 
> Simply stating or comparing the numerical values does not score.

parts.problem_md:
Wildlife researchers are studying the swimming speeds, $x \text{km h}^{-1}$, of two species of penguin, the gentoo penguin and the emperor penguin. For 40 gentoo penguins, the mean swimming speed is 31.4 $\text{km h}^{-1}$ and the standard deviation is 3.8 $\text{km h}^{-1}$.

Using $x_{G}$ to denote the swimming speeds of the gentoo penguins, show that $\sum x_{G} = 1256$ and find the value of $\sum x_{G}^{2}$.
parts.solution_md:
The sum of the speeds is the number of penguins multiplied by the mean

$40 \times 31 . 4 = 1256$

$\sum x_{G} = 1256$

**[B1]**

Use the variance formula, `\dfrac{\sum x^{2}}{n} - \left(\bar{x}\right)^{2}`, with the variance equal to the standard deviation squared

$3 . 8^{2} = \frac{\sumx_{G}^{2}}{40} - 31 . 4^{2}$

**[M1]**

Rearrange for $\sum x_{G}^{2}$

`\sum x_{G}^{2} = 40\left(14.44 + 985.96\right) = 40 \times 1000.4`

$\sum x_{G}^{2} = 40016$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 40 × 31.4 shown, leading to the given 1256.
> 
> **M1**: 3.8 squared set equal to $\frac{\sumx_{G}^{2}}{40}$ minus 31.4 squared, or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: $\sum x_{G}^{2} = 40016$.

parts.problem_md:
The swimming speeds, $x_{E} \text{km h}^{-1}$, of 20 emperor penguins are also recorded. For all 60 penguins, the mean swimming speed is 24.1 $\text{km h}^{-1}$ and $\sum x^{2} = 41891$.

Find the mean and the standard deviation of the swimming speeds of the 20 emperor penguins.
parts.solution_md:
Find the total of all 60 speeds, then subtract the gentoo total

$60 \times 24 . 1 = 1446$

$\sum x_{E} = 1446 - 1256 = 190$

$\overline{x}_{E} = \frac{190}{20}$

**Final answer:** **Mean = 9.5 **$\text{km h}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

Subtract the gentoo sum of squares from the total sum of squares in the same way

$\sum x_{E}^{2} = 41891 - 40016 = 1875$

**[B1]**

Use the variance formula for the emperor penguins

$\text{Variance} = \frac{1875}{20} - 9 . 5^{2}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 93 . 75 - 90 . 25 = 3 . 5$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{3.5} = 1 . 8708 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation = 1.87 **$\text{km h}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Emperor mean of 9.5.
> 
> **B1**: $\sum x_{E}^{2} = 1875$. Accept unevaluated.
> 
> **M1**: 1875, 20 and the emperor mean substituted into a correct variance formula, including subtracting the mean squared. Follow through from their values.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 1.87, or √3.5.

parts.problem_md:
The resting heart rates, $x$ beats per minute (bpm), of a sample of mice are summarised by

`\sum\left(x - a\right) = 150` and `\sum\left(x - a\right)^{2} = 1050`,

where $a$ is a constant.

Given that the variance of the resting heart rates is 10, find the two possible values of the number of mice in the sample.
parts.solution_md:
Let $n$ be the number of mice. Subtracting $a$ does not change the variance, so use the variance formula with the coded totals, `\dfrac{\sum\left(x - a\right)^{2}}{n} - \left(\dfrac{\sum\left(x - a\right)}{n}\right)^{2}`, and set it equal to 10

`\dfrac{1050}{n} - \left(\dfrac{150}{n}\right)^{2} = 10`

**[M1]**

Multiply through by $n^{2}$ and rearrange into a quadratic

$1050 n - 22500 = 10 n^{2}$

$n^{2} - 105 n + 2250 = 0$

**[M1]**

Factorise and solve

$( n - 30 ) ( n - 75 ) = 0$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $n = 30$** or **$n = 75$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: 1050, 150 and $n$ substituted into a correct variance formula for the coded values, including subtracting `\left(\dfrac{150}{n}\right)^{2}`, and set equal to 10.
> 
> **M1**: Fractions cleared to form a three-term quadratic in $n$.
> 
> **M1**: The quadratic solved, by factorising or the quadratic formula.
> 
> **A1**: $n = 30$ and $n = 75$.

parts.problem_md: Given also that the mean resting heart rate is 605 bpm, find the two possible values of $a$.
parts.solution_md:
The mean of $x$ is $a$ plus the mean of the coded values, $\frac{150}{n}$

$605 = a + \frac{150}{n}$

**[M1]**

When $n = 30$, find the mean of the coded values first

$\frac{150}{30} = 5$

$a = 605 - 5$

When $n = 75$

$\frac{150}{75} = 2$

$a = 605 - 2$

**Final answer:** $a = 600$** or **$a = 603$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $605 = a + \frac{150}{n}$ used with at least one of their values of $n$.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 600$ and $a = 603$. Follow through from their values of $n$.

parts.problem_md:
A teacher records the number of minutes, $t$, that a student, Hattie, is late for school each day during a school year. The results are shown in the table below.

| **Time, ***t*** (minutes)** | **Frequency ***f* |
|---|---|
| −10 ≤ *t* < −5 | 3 |
| −5 ≤ *t* < 0 | 19 |
| 0 ≤ *t* < 5 | 32 |
| 5 ≤ *t* < 10 | *a* |
| 10 ≤ *t* < 20 | 53 |
| 20 ≤ *t* < 60 | 24 |

Write down, in the context of the question, what the class −10 ≤ t < −5 represents.
parts.solution_md:
A negative number of minutes late means that Hattie arrived before school started

**Final answer:** **Hattie arrived at school between 5 and 10 minutes early**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Arriving between 5 and 10 minutes early, or equivalent in context. "Negative lateness" without explanation does not score.

parts.problem_md:
(i) Using $x$ to represent the mid-point of each class, find an expression in terms of $a$ for $\sum f x$, giving your answer in simplified form.

(ii) Given that $\sum f x$ = 2132.5 and $\sum f x^{2}$ = 53568.75, calculate estimates of the mean and the standard deviation of the number of minutes Hattie was late for school.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

The mid-points are −7.5, −2.5, 2.5, 7.5, 15 and 40. Multiply each by its frequency and add

$\sum f x = 3 ( - 7 . 5 ) + 19 ( - 2 . 5 ) + 32 ( 2 . 5 ) + 7 . 5 a + 53 ( 15 ) + 24 ( 40 )$

$\sum f x = 1765 + 7 . 5 a$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Use the given value of $\sum f x$ to find $a$, and hence the number of days

$1765 + 7 . 5 a = 2132 . 5$

$7 . 5 a = 367 . 5$

$a = 49$

$\sum f = 3 + 19 + 32 + 49 + 53 + 24 = 180$

Divide $\sum f x$ by the number of days

$\overline{x} = \frac{2132.5}{180} = 11 . 847 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Mean = 11.8 minutes (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

Use the formula for the variance, `\dfrac{\sum fx^{2}}{\sum f} - \left(\bar{x}\right)^{2}`

`\text{Variance} = \dfrac{53568.75}{180} - \left(\dfrac{2132.5}{180}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 297 . 604 \dots - 140 . 356 \dots = 157 . 248 \dots$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{157.248\dots} = 12 . 539 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation = 12.5 minutes (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $\sum f x = 1765 + 7 . 5 a$, or an equivalent simplified expression.
> 
> **B1**: Mean which rounds to 11.8, found using $a = 49$ and a total frequency of 180.
> 
> **M1**: 53568.75, their total frequency and their mean substituted into a correct variance formula, including subtracting the mean squared.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 12.5.

parts.problem_md:
Hattie notices that on three of the days recorded in the class 20 ≤ t < 60 as being 40 minutes late, she had actually arrived 40 minutes early.

Find a corrected estimate of the mean number of minutes Hattie was late for school.
parts.solution_md:
Each of the three days changes from 40 to −40, a change of −80, so subtract 3 × 80 from Σfx

$\text{Corrected} \sum f x = 2132 . 5 - 3 \times 80 = 1892 . 5$

The number of days is still 180

$\overline{x} = \frac{1892.5}{180}$

**[M1]**

$\overline{x} = 10 . 513 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Corrected mean = 10.5 minutes (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: 240 subtracted from 2132.5 (three values of 40 replaced by −40) and the result divided by their total frequency.
> 
> **A1**: Corrected mean which rounds to 10.5.

parts.problem_md:
Two friends, Anna and Connor, are playing a game on their phones. As they play, they can buy three different boosters, each at a fixed cost. The numbers of purchases they each make are shown in the table below.

|   | **Super-charge** | **Re-energise** | **Level-up** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Anna** | 4 | 0 | 2 |
| **Connor** | 3 | 6 | 1 |

(i) The mean and the standard deviation of the costs, in dollars, of Anna's purchases are 0.50 and 0 respectively. Write down the cost, in dollars, of a single Level-up purchase.

(ii) Given that the mean cost, in dollars, of Connor's purchases is 0.38, find the standard deviation of the costs of Connor's purchases.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

A standard deviation of 0 means there is no spread, so every one of Anna's purchases costs the same as her mean

**Final answer:** **A Level-up purchase costs 0.50 dollars**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Super-charge also costs 0.50 dollars, from Anna's purchases. Let a Re-energise purchase cost $R$ dollars. Connor makes 10 purchases with a mean of 0.38, so his total is 3.80

$3 ( 0 . 50 ) + 6 R + 1 ( 0 . 50 ) = 10 \times 0 . 38$

**[M1]**

$2 + 6 R = 3 . 8$

$6 R = 1 . 8$

$R = 0 . 30$

**[A1]**

Connor's 10 purchases are four at 0.50 and six at 0.30. Use the formula for the variance, `\dfrac{\sum x^{2}}{n} - \left(\bar{x}\right)^{2}`

$\text{Variance} = \frac{4\times0.50^{2}+6\times0.30^{2}}{10} - 0 . 38^{2}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 0 . 154 - 0 . 1444 = 0 . 0096$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{0.0096} = 0 . 097979 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation = 0.0980 dollars (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 0.50 dollars (50 cents).
> 
> **M1**: An equation for the cost of a Re-energise purchase using Connor's total of 3.80 (or mean of 0.38) and the cost of 0.50 for the other two boosters.
> 
> **A1**: Re-energise costs 0.30 dollars.
> 
> **M1**: Connor's costs substituted into a correct variance formula, including subtracting the mean squared. Follow through from an incorrect Re-energise cost.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 0.0980. Accept 9.80 cents.

parts.problem_md:
The speeds, $x$ miles per hour, of a sample of cars passing a house on a road with a speed limit of 30 miles per hour are recorded. The speeds are summarised by

`\sum\left(x - 30\right)` = 13.4 and `\sum\left(x - 30\right)^{2} = 1470`.

State, with a reason, whether the mean speed of the cars in the sample is greater than or less than the speed limit.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Greater than the speed limit, because Σ(x − 30) is positive, so the mean of x − 30 is positive and the mean speed is more than 30 mph**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: "Greater", with a reason referring to `\sum\left(x - 30\right)` being positive (so the mean of $x - 30$ is positive).

parts.problem_md: Given that the mean speed of the cars in the sample is 30.67 miles per hour, find the standard deviation of $x$.
parts.solution_md:
The mean of $x - 30$ is 0.67, which gives the number of cars

$\frac{13.4}{n} = 0 . 67$

$n = 20$

**[B1]**

Subtracting 30 does not change the spread, so use the variance formula with the coded totals, `\dfrac{\sum\left(x - 30\right)^{2}}{n} - \left(\dfrac{\sum\left(x - 30\right)}{n}\right)^{2}`

`\text{Variance} = \dfrac{1470}{20} - \left(\dfrac{13.4}{20}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 73 . 5 - 0 . 4489 = 73 . 0511$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{73.0511} = 8 . 5470 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation = 8.55 mph (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Number of cars, $n = 20$.
> 
> **M1**: 1470, their $n$ and 0.67 substituted into a correct variance formula for the coded values, including subtracting the square of the coded mean.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 8.55.

parts.problem_md:
The median speed of the cars in the sample is 27.43 miles per hour.

State, with a reason, the type of skewness of the speeds, and state what the median tells you about the speeds of the cars compared with the speed limit.
parts.solution_md:
Compare the mean with the median

*The mean (30.67 mph) is greater than the median (27.43 mph)*

**Final answer:** **The speeds are positively skewed, because the mean is greater than the median: a few very fast cars raise the mean**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **The median is below 30 mph, so at least half of the cars were travelling below the speed limit**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Positive skew (or positively skewed), with a reason such as the mean being greater than the median. "Skewed" or "not symmetrical" without the direction does not score.
> 
> **B1**: At least half (or most) of the cars were below the speed limit, because the median is less than 30. Must refer to the speed limit or to 30 mph.

parts.problem_md:
A group of people recorded the length of time, $t$ hours, that they spent browsing the internet on a particular day. The results are summarised in the table below.

| **Time, ***t*** (hours)** | **Frequency, ***f* |
|---|---|
| 0 < t ≤ 2 | 3 |
| 2 < t ≤ 4 | 5 |
| 4 < t ≤ 6 | *a* |
| 6 < t ≤ 8 | 10 |
| 8 < t ≤ 10 | 2 |

An estimate of the mean time spent browsing the internet is 5 hours and 15 minutes.

Find the value of $a$, and calculate an estimate of the variance of the time spent browsing the internet.
parts.solution_md:
Write the mean in hours, since the times are in hours

$5 + \frac{15}{60} = 5 . 25$

Use the mid-points 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 to write the estimated mean in terms of $a$

$\frac{3\times1+5\times3+5a+10\times7+2\times9}{20+a} = 5 . 25$

**[M1]**

Multiply both sides by $20 + a$ and solve

$106 + 5 a = 105 + 5 . 25 a$

$0 . 25 a = 1$

$a = 4$

**[A1]**

There are now 24 people. Find $\sum x^{2} f$ with the same mid-points

$\sum x^{2} f = 3 \times 1^{2} + 5 \times 3^{2} + 4 \times 5^{2} + 10 \times 7^{2} + 2 \times 9^{2} = 800$

Use the formula for the variance, `\dfrac{\sum x^{2}f}{\sum f} - \left(\bar{x}\right)^{2}`

$\text{Variance} = \frac{800}{24} - 5 . 25^{2}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 33 . 333 \dots - 27 . 5625 = 5 . 7708 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Variance = 5.77 hours² (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Mid-points and frequencies, including $a$, substituted into the formula for the mean with $20 + a$ as the denominator, and set equal to 5.25. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 4$.
> 
> **M1**: Mid-points and frequencies (with their value of $a$) substituted into a correct variance formula, including subtracting the mean squared.
> 
> **A1**: Variance which rounds to 5.77, or $\frac{277}{48}$. Units are not required.

parts.problem_md:
$a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are 4 integers written in order of size, starting with the smallest.

The sum of $a$, $b$ and $c$ is 70.

The mean of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ is 25.

The range of the 4 integers is 14.

Work out the median of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$.
parts.solution_md:
The mean of the four integers is 25, so their total is 4 times 25

$a + b + c + d = 4 \times 25 = 100$

**[M1]**

The sum of $a$, $b$ and $c$ is 70

$d = 100 - 70$

$d = 30$

**[A1]**

The integers are in order, so the range is $d - a$

$30 - a = 14$

$a = 16$

Use the total again to find the sum of the two middle integers

$b + c = 100 - 16 - 30 = 54$

**[M1]**

The median of four ordered integers is halfway between the 2nd and 3rd, $b$ and $c$

$\text{Median} = \frac{b+c}{2} = \frac{54}{2}$

**Final answer:** **Median = 27**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Total of the four integers found as 100 from the mean.
> 
> **A1**: $d = 30$.
> 
> **M1**: Range used to find $a = 16$, then $b + c$ found from the total.
> 
> **A1**: Median of 27.

parts.problem_md:
A machine is set to fill sacks of potatoes to a target weight of 50 kg, although the actual weight, $w$ kg, of a sack can vary. To test the machine, a random sample of 20 sacks is taken, and the weights are summarised by

`\sum\left(w - 50\right) = 20` and `\sum\left(w - 50\right)^{2} = 220`.

Find the exact values of the mean and the standard deviation of $w$.
parts.solution_md:
Find the mean of the coded values $w - 50$

`\dfrac{\sum\left(w - 50\right)}{n} = \dfrac{20}{20} = 1`

Add 50 back on to find the mean weight

$\overline{w} = 50 + 1$

**Final answer:** **Mean = 51 kg**

**[B1]**

Subtracting 50 from every weight does not change the spread, so use the variance formula with the coded totals, `\dfrac{\sum\left(w - 50\right)^{2}}{n} - \left(\dfrac{\sum\left(w - 50\right)}{n}\right)^{2}`

`\text{Variance} = \dfrac{220}{20} - \left(\dfrac{20}{20}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 11 - 1 = 10$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

**Final answer:** $\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{10}$** kg**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Mean of 51.
> 
> **M1**: 220, 20 and 20 substituted into a correct variance formula for the coded values, including subtracting the square of the coded mean. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation of $\sqrt{10}$. Also accept answers which round to 3.16.

parts.problem_md:
Find the value of

(i) $\sum w$,

(ii) $\sum w^{2}$.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

The sum of the weights is the number of sacks multiplied by the mean

$\sum w = 20 \times 51$

$\sum w = 1020$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Use the variance formula for $w$ itself, `\dfrac{\sum w^{2}}{n} - \left(\bar{w}\right)^{2}`, with the variance from part (a)

$10 = \frac{\sumw^{2}}{20} - 51^{2}$

**[M1]**

Rearrange for $\sum w^{2}$

$\sum w^{2} = 20 ( 10 + 51^{2} )$

$\sum w^{2} = 52220$

parts.problem_md:
Two archers, $A$ and $B$, compete in an archery match. Each archer shoots three arrows in each of five rounds, and the archer with the higher total score over the five rounds wins.

The scores, $x$, for the five rounds are coded using $d = x - 25$, and the coded scores are summarised as follows.

Archer $A$: $\sum d = - 2$ and $\sum d^{2} = 6$

Archer $B$: $\sum d = 6$ and $\sum d^{2} = 26$

Explain how, without any calculation, you can tell that archer $B$ won the match.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Both archers' scores are coded by subtracting 25 from each of the same number of rounds, so the archer with the larger total of d has the larger total score, and 6 is greater than −2**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: An explanation that the same amount (25) is subtracted from each of five scores for both archers, so the larger $\sum d$ (6 for $B$, compared with −2 for $A$) means the larger total score.

parts.problem_md: Find the mean and the standard deviation of the scores for each archer.
parts.solution_md:
Find the mean of the coded scores for archer $A$, $\frac{\sumd}{5}$

$\frac{\sumd}{5} = \frac{-2}{5} = - 0 . 4$

Add 25 back on to find the mean score

`\bar{x}_{A} = 25 + \left(-0.4\right)`

**Final answer:** **Mean for A = 24.6**

**[B1]**

Do the same for archer $B$

$\frac{\sumd}{5} = \frac{6}{5} = 1 . 2$

$\overline{x}_{B} = 25 + 1 . 2$

**Final answer:** **Mean for B = 26.2**

**[B1]**

Subtracting 25 does not change the spread, so find each variance from the coded totals, using `\dfrac{\sum d^{2}}{n} - \left(\dfrac{\sum d}{n}\right)^{2}`

`\text{Variance for } A = \dfrac{6}{5} - \left(\dfrac{-2}{5}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance for} A = 1 . 2 - 0 . 16 = 1 . 04$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\text{Standard deviation for} A = \sqrt{1.04} = 1 . 0198 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation for A = 1.02 (3 s.f.)**

Do the same for archer $B$

`\text{Variance for } B = \dfrac{26}{5} - \left(\dfrac{6}{5}\right)^{2}`

$\text{Variance for} B = 5 . 2 - 1 . 44 = 3 . 76$

$\text{Standard deviation for} B = \sqrt{3.76} = 1 . 9390 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation for B = 1.94 (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Mean for $A$ of 24.6.
> 
> **B1**: Mean for $B$ of 26.2.
> 
> **M1**: The coded totals substituted into a correct variance formula for at least one archer, including subtracting the square of the coded mean.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviations which round to 1.02 for $A$ and 1.94 for $B$.

parts.problem_md: Compare the scores of the two archers.
parts.solution_md:
Compare the means, then the standard deviations, in context

**Final answer:** **On average, archer B scored more per round than archer A**

**[B1]**

parts.problem_md:
The speeds, $s$ miles per hour, of 80 vehicles passing a speed camera were recorded and are summarised in the table below.

| **Speed, ***s*** (mph)** | 20 ≤ s < 25 | 25 ≤ s < 30 | 30 ≤ s < 35 | s ≥ 35 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Number of vehicles** | 23 | 48 | 7 | 2 |

(i) Write down the modal class for these data.

(ii) Write down the class that contains the median.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

The three closed classes have equal widths, and the class with the highest frequency, 48, is

$25 \leq s < 30$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The median of 80 speeds lies between the 40th and 41st in order. The cumulative frequencies are

*23, 71, 78, 80*

so the 40th and 41st speeds are both in the second class

$25 \leq s < 30$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Modal class $25 \leq s < 30$. Accept "25 to 30". The frequency 48 on its own does not score.
> 
> **B1**: Median class $25 \leq s < 30$.
> 
> The two answers are marked independently.

parts.problem_md:
(i) Assuming that $s \geq 35$ means $35 \leq s < 40$, calculate an estimate of the mean speed of the 80 vehicles.

(ii) It is now discovered that $s \geq 35$ means $35 \leq s < 60$. Without further calculation, state with a reason whether this would cause an increase, a decrease or no change to the estimated mean.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

Use the mid-point of each class to represent the speeds in it

*Mid-points: 22.5, 27.5, 32.5, 37.5*

**[B1]**

Multiply each mid-point by its frequency, add, and divide by 80

$\overline{s} = \frac{23\times22.5+48\times27.5+7\times32.5+2\times37.5}{80} = \frac{2140}{80}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **Mean = 26.75 mph**

**[A1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **Increase, because the mid-point of the top class rises from 37.5 to 47.5, which increases the total of the speeds while the number of vehicles stays at 80**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: At least 3 correct mid-points seen. Mid-points 0.5 lower (22, 27, 32, 37) are also accepted.
> 
> **M1**: Mid-points multiplied by frequencies, added and divided by 80. Accept unevaluated. One error in a mid-point is condoned, but not an omitted class.
> 
> **A1**: Mean of 26.75, or 26.8 to 3 significant figures.
> 
> **B1**: "Increase", with a reason referring to the larger mid-point (or larger values) of the top class. "Increase" with no reason does not score.

parts.problem_md:
The ages, $x$ years, of the 200 people attending a vaccination clinic on one day are summarised by

$\sum x = 7211$ and $\sum x^{2} = 275360$.

Calculate the mean and the standard deviation of the ages of these people.
parts.solution_md:
Divide the sum of the ages by 200

$\overline{x} = \frac{7211}{200}$

**Final answer:** **Mean = 36.055 years**

**[B1]**

Use the formula for the variance, `\dfrac{\sum x^{2}}{n} - \left(\bar{x}\right)^{2}`

`\text{Variance} = \dfrac{275360}{200} - \left(\dfrac{7211}{200}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 1376 . 8 - 1299 . 963025 = 76 . 836975$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{76.836975} = 8 . 7656 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation = 8.77 years (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Mean of 36.055, or 36.1 to 3 significant figures.
> 
> **M1**: 275360, 200 and the mean substituted into a correct variance formula, including subtracting the mean squared. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 8.77.

parts.problem_md:
One person leaves the clinic without being vaccinated, and their age is removed from the data. The mean age of the remaining 199 people is exactly 36 years.

Find the age of the person who left, and the standard deviation of the ages of the remaining 199 people.
parts.solution_md:
The total age of the remaining people is 199 multiplied by their mean

$199 \times 36 = 7164$

The age removed is the difference between the two totals

$7211 - 7164$

**Final answer:** **The person who left is 47 years old**

**[B1]**

Remove the square of this age from $\sum x^{2}$

$\sum x^{2} = 275360 - 47^{2} = 273151$

**[B1]**

Use the variance formula for the remaining 199 people, whose mean is 36

$\text{Variance} = \frac{273151}{199} - 36^{2}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 76 . 618 \dots$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{76.618\dots} = 8 . 7531 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation = 8.75 years (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Age of 47.
> 
> **B1**: New $\sum x^{2}$ of 273151. Accept unevaluated, such as $275360 - 47^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: New $\sum x^{2}$, 199 and the new mean of 36 substituted into a correct variance formula, including subtracting the mean squared. Follow through from an incorrect age.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 8.75.

parts.problem_md:
The time, $t$ minutes, that each of 100 people spent exercising on a particular day is summarised in the table below.

| **Time, ***t*** (minutes)** | **Frequency ***f* |
|---|---|
| 0 ≤ t ≤ 10 | 1 |
| 10 < t ≤ 20 | 12 |
| 20 < t ≤ 30 | 25 |
| 30 < t ≤ 40 | *a* |
| 40 < t ≤ 50 | *b* |
| 50 < t ≤ 60 | 14 |

Given that an estimate of the mean time spent exercising is 35.4 minutes, find the values of $a$ and $b$.
parts.solution_md:
The frequencies add up to 100

$1 + 12 + 25 + a + b + 14 = 100$

$a + b = 48$

**[B1]**

Use the mid-points 5, 15, 25, 35, 45 and 55 to write the estimated mean in terms of $a$ and $b$

$\frac{1\times5+12\times15+25\times25+35a+45b+14\times55}{100} = 35 . 4$

**[M1]**

$1580 + 35 a + 45 b = 3540$

$7 a + 9 b = 392$

Multiply $a + b = 48$ by 7 and subtract, to eliminate $a$

$7 a + 9 b - ( 7 a + 7 b ) = 392 - 336$

$2 b = 56$

**[M1]**

$b = 28$

Substitute back into $a + b = 48$

$a = 20$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $a + b = 48$, or an equivalent equation from the total frequency.
> 
> **M1**: Mid-points and frequencies substituted into the formula for the mean and set equal to 35.4. Accept unsimplified. Mid-points 0.5 higher or lower are accepted for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: A valid method to solve the two equations for both unknowns, by elimination or substitution.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 20$ and $b = 28$.

parts.problem_md:
A machine is set to fill sacks of potatoes to a target weight of 50 kg. The weights, $w$ kg, of a random sample of 7 sacks are summarised by

$\sum ( w - 50 )$ = −14.6.

Show that the mean weight of the sacks in the sample is 47.9 kg, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solution_md:
Find the mean of the coded values $w - 50$

`\dfrac{\sum\left(w - 50\right)}{n} = \dfrac{-14.6}{7} = -2.0857\ldots`

Add 50 back on to find the mean weight

`\bar{w} = 50 + \left(-2.0857\ldots\right)`

**[M1]**

$\overline{w} = 47 . 914 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Mean = 47.9 kg (3 s.f.), as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $\frac{-14.6}{7}$ added to 50. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: An unrounded value such as 47.914 seen before the given answer of 47.9. As the answer is given, the working must be shown.

parts.problem_md: Given also that `\sum\left(w - 50\right)^{2}` = 170.2, find the standard deviation of the weights of these 7 sacks.
parts.solution_md:
Subtracting 50 from every weight does not change the spread, so use the variance formula with the coded totals, `\dfrac{\sum\left(w - 50\right)^{2}}{n} - \left(\dfrac{\sum(w - 50)}{n}\right)^{2}`

`\text{Variance} = \dfrac{170.2}{7} - \left(\dfrac{-14.6}{7}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 24 . 3142 \dots - 4 . 3502 \dots = 19 . 9640 \dots$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{19.9640\dots} = 4 . 4681 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation = 4.47 kg (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: 170.2, −14.6 and 7 substituted into a correct variance formula for the coded values, including subtracting the square of the coded mean. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 4.47.

parts.problem_md:
The times, $t$ seconds, taken by 8 speed skaters to finish a 1000 m race are summarised by

Find the mean and the standard deviation of these times.

$\overline{t} = 75 + 4 . 25$

**Final answer:** **Mean = 79.25 seconds**

`\text{Variance} = \dfrac{212}{8} - \left(\dfrac{34}{8}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 8 . 4375$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{8.4375} = 2 . 9047 \dots$

> 
> **A1**: Mean of 79.25.

> **M1**: 212, 34 and 8 substituted into a correct variance formula for the coded values, including subtracting `\left(\dfrac{34}{8}\right)^{2}`. Accept unsimplified.

parts.problem_md:
The lengths, $l$ cm, of a sample of nine otters, measured to the nearest centimetre by a wildlife research team, are as follows.

76, 77, 91, 65, 63, 83, 92, 61, 88

Calculate the mean and the standard deviation of these nine lengths.
parts.solution_md:
Add the nine lengths and divide by 9

$\sum l = 76 + 77 + 91 + 65 + 63 + 83 + 92 + 61 + 88 = 696$

$\overline{l} = \frac{696}{9}$

$\overline{l} = 77 . 333 \dots$

$\sum l^{2} = 76^{2} + 77^{2} + 91^{2} + 65^{2} + 63^{2} + 83^{2} + 92^{2} + 61^{2} + 88^{2} = 54998$

Use the formula for the variance, `\dfrac{\sum l^{2}}{n} - \left(\bar{l}\right)^{2}`

`\text{Variance} = \dfrac{54998}{9} - \left(\dfrac{696}{9}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 130 . 44 \dots$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{130.44\dots} = 11 . 421 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation = 11.4 cm (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Mean of $\frac{232}{3}$, or answers which round to 77.3.
> 
> **M1**: $\sum l^{2}$ (or the squared lengths), 9 and the mean substituted into a correct variance formula, including subtracting the mean squared. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 11.4.
>

parts.problem_md:

$\frac{56+58}{2}$

$\frac{62+64}{2}$

> **B1**: Median of 57.

parts.problem_md:
The advertising department at Coffee4Life designs an advert which says:

parts.problem_md:
Fran sits three Mathematics papers and six Science papers in her final examinations. Each of the nine papers is weighted equally.

Her mean mark on the three Mathematics papers is 62.7%. To gain a place at her chosen university, she needs an overall mean mark of 78.5% across all nine papers. Her mean mark on four of her Science papers is 84.2%.

Calculate the mean mark Fran must achieve on her final two Science papers to gain a place at university.
parts.solution_md:
Multiply each mean by its number of papers to find the total marks so far

$\text{Mathematics total} = 3 \times 62 . 7 = 188 . 1$

$\text{Science total (4 papers)} = 4 \times 84 . 2 = 336 . 8$

**[B1]**

Find the total needed across all nine papers in the same way

$\text{Total needed} = 9 \times 78 . 5 = 706 . 5$

**[B1]**

Subtract the totals so far from the total needed, then share the remainder between the last two papers

$\text{Total for last 2 papers} = 706 . 5 - 188 . 1 - 336 . 8 = 181 . 6$

$\text{Mean needed} = \frac{181.6}{2}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **Mean mark needed = 90.8%**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both known totals, 188.1 and 336.8, found. Accept unevaluated.
> 
> **B1**: Required total of 706.5 found. Accept unevaluated.
> 
> **M1**: Known totals subtracted from the required total and the result divided by 2. Accept an equation such as 3 × 62.7 + 4 × 84.2 + 2m = 9 × 78.5.
>

parts.problem_md:
A factory aims to produce 500 plastic garden chairs per day. The number of chairs made per day, $c$, over a period of 10 working days is summarised by

`\sum\left(c - 500\right) = -15` and `\sum\left(c - 500\right)^{2} = 381`.

Find the mean number of chairs made per day over the 10 days.
parts.solution_md:
Find the mean of the coded values $c - 500$

`\dfrac{\sum\left(c - 500\right)}{n} = \dfrac{-15}{10} = -1.5`

Add 500 back on to find the mean number of chairs

`\bar{c} = 500 + \left(-1.5\right)`

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **Mean = 498.5 chairs per day**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $\frac{-15}{10}$ added to 500. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: Mean of 498.5.

parts.problem_md: Find the standard deviation of the number of chairs made per day over the 10 days.
parts.solution_md:
Subtracting 500 from every value does not change the spread, so use the variance formula with the coded totals, `\dfrac{\sum\left(c - 500\right)^{2}}{n} - \left(\dfrac{\sum\left(c - 500\right)}{n}\right)^{2}`

`\text{Variance} = \dfrac{381}{10} - \left(\dfrac{-15}{10}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

$\text{Variance} = 38 . 1 - 2 . 25 = 35 . 85$

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

$\text{Standard deviation} = \sqrt{35.85} = 5 . 9874 \dots$

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation = 5.99 chairs (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: 381, −15 and 10 substituted into a correct variance formula for the coded values, including subtracting the square of the coded mean. Accept unsimplified.
> 
> **A1**: Standard deviation which rounds to 5.99.

parts.problem_md:

parts.problem_md:

parts.problem_md: Calculate an estimate of the standard deviation of the number of goals scored per team.
parts.solution_md:

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance

**Final answer:** **Standard deviation = 2.78 goals (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Mid-points and frequencies substituted into a correct variance formula, including subtracting the square of the mean from part (a). Accept unsimplified.
>
